concepts.name: Project Tiger: Origin, Legal Basis and Institutional Evolution
key_dimensions: Launched in 1973 under Wildlife Protection Act 1972 — NOT a standalone legislation
Transformation from administrative scheme to statutory backing via WLPA Amendment 2006 (Chapter IVB)
Shift from Forest Department control to dedicated National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA)
UPSC trap: Project Tiger predates NTCA by 33 years — often confused as co-originating

concepts.name: National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA): Composition, Powers and Statutory Status
key_dimensions: Statutory body under Wildlife Protection Act 1972 (Section 38L), NOT a constitutional body
Chaired by Minister of Environment, Forest and Climate Change; Vice-Chair is Minister of State
Powers include approving Tiger Conservation Plans, monitoring, and advising state governments
UPSC trap: NTCA cannot override state governments but can recommend withdrawal of reserve status — distinction from CEC

concepts.name: Tiger Reserve: Legal Definition, Declaration Process and Zoning Structure
key_dimensions: Declared by State Government on recommendation of NTCA under Section 38V of WLPA 1972
Mandatory two-zone structure: Core/Critical Tiger Habitat (CTH) and Buffer Zone — legally distinct treatment
Core zone: inviolate, no human activity except conservation; Buffer zone: co-existence model allowed
UPSC trap: Tiger Reserve ≠ National Park ≠ Wildlife Sanctuary — overlapping boundaries are common but legally separate designations

concepts.name: Critical Tiger Habitat (CTH): Legal Provision, Inviolability and Tribal Rights Conflict
key_dimensions: Defined under Section 38V(4) of WLPA 1972 — areas where co-existence is scientifically deemed impossible
Relocation of communities from CTH must be voluntary and with free, prior, informed consent per Forest Rights Act 2006
Tension between WLPA 1972 and Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act 2006
UPSC trap: FRA 2006 rights CANNOT be extinguished merely by CTH notification — Supreme Court clarification in Niyamgiri-type precedents

concepts.name: Tiger Conservation Plan (TCP): Mandatory Requirement and Components
key_dimensions: Mandatory under Section 38V(2) for every Tiger Reserve — must be prepared by state government
Must include: site-specific plan for CTH, buffer zone management, relocation packages, monitoring protocols
Approved by NTCA — a procedural check that UPSC may test as 'which body approves'
Absence or non-compliance with TCP can be grounds for legal challenge to reserve activities

concepts.name: Buffer Zone Management: Eco-Sensitive Zone vs. Buffer Zone Distinction
key_dimensions: Buffer Zone under WLPA 1972 ≠ Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ) under Environment Protection Act 1986 — different legal instruments
Buffer zone allows regulated human use, tourism, and community conservation activities
ESZ is declared by MoEFCC around Protected Areas; can overlap with buffer zone but is separately notified
UPSC trap: ESZ is mandatory around National Parks/Sanctuaries (SC ruling 2022 — minimum 1 km), NOT automatically around Tiger Reserves

concepts.name: Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB) vs. NTCA: Roles in Tiger Protection
key_dimensions: WCCB is a statutory body under MoEFCC for combating wildlife crime — NOT tiger-specific
NTCA focuses on habitat management, monitoring, and policy; WCCB focuses on enforcement and intelligence
Both operate under MoEFCC but have distinct mandates — often confused in MCQs
CITES implementation in India is coordinated through WCCB, not NTCA

concepts.name: Tiger Census Methodology: All-India Tiger Estimation
key_dimensions: Conducted every 4 years by Wildlife Institute of India (WII) in collaboration with NTCA and state governments
Uses camera trap density estimation, pugmark (now phased out), and occupancy modeling — MSTrIPES app for monitoring
India's 2022 census: ~3,682 tigers — largest wild tiger population globally (>70% of world's tigers)
UPSC trap: Census conducted by WII (an autonomous institute under MoEFCC), NOT directly by NTCA or Forest Survey of India

concepts.name: Wildlife Institute of India (WII): Role, Status and Functions in Tiger Conservation
key_dimensions: Autonomous institution under MoEFCC, located in Dehradun — NOT a statutory body under WLPA
Conducts tiger census, prepares landscape-level conservation plans, and provides technical support to NTCA
Distinct from NTCA (statutory), Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (enforcement), and FSI (forest cover assessment)
UPSC trap: WII ≠ NTCA ≠ FSI — each has different legal character and functional mandate

concepts.name: Tiger Corridors: Concept, Legal Status and Connectivity Challenges
key_dimensions: Tiger corridors are NOT separately designated under any law — they are management/planning constructs
Identified in National Tiger Conservation Authority's Landscape-level plans and TCP buffer zones
Major corridors: Terai Arc Landscape, Central Indian Landscape, Western Ghats Landscape
UPSC angle: Corridors cross state boundaries, revenue lands, and private areas — legal protection remains a gap; no dedicated corridor legislation exists

concepts.name: States with Highest Tiger Population vs. States with Most Tiger Reserves: The Distinction
key_dimensions: Madhya Pradesh has highest tiger population (2022 census) — 'Tiger State of India'
Most Tiger Reserves by number: varies — Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh among top; check current count (~54 reserves as of 2023)
Maharashtra and Uttarakhand also significant — UPSC may ask 'which state has most reserves' vs. 'most tigers'
UPSC trap: State with most reserves ≠ state with most tigers — MP leads in population, not necessarily in reserve count

concepts.name: Relocation and Rehabilitation of Communities from Tiger Reserves: Legal Framework
key_dimensions: Must comply with both WLPA 1972 (Section 38V) and Forest Rights Act 2006 simultaneously
Compensation package: minimum Rs. 10 lakh per family (revised periodically) or land-for-land
Relocation is VOLUNTARY from CTH — coercive relocation is illegal post-FRA 2006
UPSC trap: Gram Sabha consent is mandatory under FRA 2006 even when WLPA mandates inviolate status of CTH — both laws must be reconciled

concepts.name: International Frameworks Supporting Tiger Conservation: TX2 Goal and St. Petersburg Declaration
key_dimensions: St. Petersburg Declaration (2010) — 13 tiger range countries pledged to double tiger numbers by 2022 (TX2 goal)
India achieved TX2 goal 4 years early (by 2018 census) — significant diplomatic and conservation milestone
Global Tiger Forum (GTF) — intergovernmental body; India is a member; secretariat in New Delhi
UPSC trap: TX2 is NOT a UN treaty — it is a political declaration; CITES is the binding international instrument for tiger trade ban

concepts.name: CITES and Tigers: Appendix Listing, Trade Ban and India's Role
key_dimensions: Tiger (Panthera tigris) listed in CITES Appendix I — strictest prohibition on international commercial trade
Appendix I listing means: trade allowed only in exceptional non-commercial circumstances with both export and import permits
India is a CITES signatory; domestic trade governed by WLPA Schedule I (equivalent protection level)
UPSC trap: CITES Appendix I does NOT ban all use — only 'commercial trade'; also does not govern domestic trade within a country

concepts.name: Schedule I of Wildlife Protection Act 1972: Tiger's Legal Protection Status
key_dimensions: Tiger listed under Schedule I of WLPA 1972 — highest protection, hunting/trade absolutely prohibited
Schedule I species cannot be hunted even in self-defense except under specific Chief Wildlife Warden order
Penalty for hunting Schedule I species: imprisonment up to 7 years + fine (enhanced post-2003 amendment)
UPSC trap: Schedule I listing under WLPA is domestic protection; CITES Appendix I is international — both apply independently to tigers

concepts.name: Sariska and Panna Tiger Reserves: Lessons from Local Extinction and Reintroduction
key_dimensions: Sariska (Rajasthan) — tigers became locally extinct by 2004–05 due to poaching; first reintroduction of tigers in India from Ranthambore
Panna (Madhya Pradesh) — tigers disappeared by 2009; reintroduction from Kanha and Bandhavgarh
Both cases highlighted failure of monitoring, political interference, and poaching network — led to NTCA reforms post-2006
UPSC angle: These are cited as case studies for importance of CTH inviolability, anti-poaching measures, and independent monitoring

concepts.name: MSTrIPES: Monitoring System for Tigers — Intensive Protection and Ecological Status
key_dimensions: Mobile-based application developed by WII for real-time patrol monitoring inside Tiger Reserves
Records patrol effort, wildlife sightings, threat data — feeds into national tiger monitoring database
Mandatory for all Tiger Reserves — part of NTCA's standardized monitoring framework
UPSC trap: MSTrIPES is a monitoring/patrolling tool, NOT a census tool — All-India Tiger Estimation uses separate camera-trap methodology

concepts.name: Human-Tiger Conflict: Compensation Mechanism and Legal Provisions
key_dimensions: Compensation for livestock/crop loss and human death/injury — paid by State Government under respective State Wildlife/Compensation schemes
No uniform national compensation law — states have varying rates; NTCA issues advisory guidelines only
Problematic tigers can be declared 'man-eaters' by Chief Wildlife Warden — only then can hunting/translocation be ordered
UPSC trap: Decision to shoot a Schedule I animal (including tiger) can ONLY be taken by Chief Wildlife Warden, NOT by District Collector or Forest Range Officer

concepts.name: Central Empowered Committee (CEC) vs. NTCA: Oversight Roles in Tiger Reserve Matters
key_dimensions: CEC is a Supreme Court-appointed committee (not statutory) to oversee forest and wildlife matters — reports to SC
NTCA is a statutory body under WLPA 1972 — reports to Parliament via MoEFCC
Any diversion of forest land within Tiger Reserve requires NTCA's approval AND Forest Conservation Act 1980 clearance
UPSC trap: CEC oversees compliance with SC orders on forests; NTCA gives statutory clearances — both may be involved in Tiger Reserve land diversion cases but through different legal channels

concepts.name: Tourism Regulation in Tiger Reserves: Core vs. Buffer Zone Rules
key_dimensions: Tourism in CTH (Core Zone) is strictly prohibited as per NTCA guidelines — only conservation-related activity permitted
Buffer zone allows regulated eco-tourism; states prepare tourism master plans as part of TCP
Supreme Court (2012) — temporary ban on tiger tourism in core areas; subsequently modified to allow regulated tourism
UPSC trap: States have autonomy in regulating buffer zone tourism but CANNOT permit tourism in Core/CTH — this is a non-negotiable restriction under NTCA norms
